verses.context: The third ‘awake’ in a row. In 51:9 the prophet cried to the arm of the LORD to awake; in 51:17 God called Jerusalem to rouse herself from the cup of his wrath; now Zion is told to wake, dress in strength and beauty, shake off the dust, and take her seat. Verse 2 reverses 47:1, where Babylon, the proud virgin daughter, was ordered down into the dust: the two cities trade places.
verses.grammar: Uri uri, "Awake, awake", is a doubled feminine imperative, followed by livshi, "clothe yourself", twice: Zion puts on strength (oz) as a garment and her bigdei tifartekh, ‘garments of your beauty’, perhaps festival or bridal clothes. Arel vetame, ‘uncircumcised and unclean’, name the foreign occupier and the ritually defiled, who will no longer enter. In verse 2 hitnaari, "Shake off", is a Hithpael, ‘shake yourself’, and qumi shevi, "Rise up and sit", pairs two imperatives: rise from the dust and sit enthroned. Shviyah bat-Tsiyyon, ‘captive daughter Zion’, uses a noun that means a captive or captivity.
verses.text: "Remove the chains" follows the Masoretes' reading (the qere), hitpattechi, a feminine imperative, ‘loose yourself’. The written text (the ketiv) has hitpattechu, ‘the chains of your neck have loosened themselves’. The difference is a single letter; both readings end with Zion free.

theology.note: Jerusalem is called ir haqqodesh, "the holy city", and the promise is that nothing unclean will enter it again. Revelation's new Jerusalem takes up the same promise: nothing unclean will ever enter it (Revelation 21:27). Holiness here is God's gift to the city, not an achievement it maintains.

verses.context: God explains the logic of the rescue in the language of the slave market. Israel was sold for nothing and will be bought back without money. Verse 4 surveys the history: Israel went down to Egypt as guests and became slaves, and Assyria oppressed them without cause. No one paid God for his people, so no one can claim to own them.
verses.grammar: Chinnam nimkartem, "You were sold for nothing", uses a Niphal (passive) perfect, and velo vekhesef tiggaelu, "without money you will be redeemed", a Niphal imperfect of gaal, the verb of the kinsman-redeemer who buys back a relative's freedom or land (Leviticus 25:25, 48). The logic is legal: since God never received a price when he handed his people over (Judges 2:14 speaks of him selling them into their enemies' hands), he owes none to recover them. In verse 4 lagur sham, "to live" there, is to sojourn as a resident alien, and beefes, "without cause", is literally ‘for nothing’, matching chinnam in verse 3.

theology.note: Redemption in Isaiah is God acting as kinsman to buy back his own. That no silver changes hands does not mean the redemption is costless: the chapter moves straight into the Servant who suffers (52:13 to 53:12). Peter says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19).

verses.context: The third stage of the history is now, and God asks what he has here: his people taken away for nothing, their rulers howling, and his own name despised all day long. The dishonor to his name, not only the suffering of his people, is the reason he will act.
verses.grammar: Mah-li-fo, ‘what do I have here?’, is a colloquial question, God surveying the scene. Luqqach ammi chinnam, "My people have been taken without cause", uses a Pual perfect, passive, and chinnam again. Moshlav yeheililu, ‘his rulers wail’, may describe the lament of Israel's own leaders or the triumphant howling of their captors; the text is uncertain and the ancient versions differ. Shemi minnoats, ‘my name is despised’, uses an unusual passive participle of naats, to treat with contempt.

theology.note: God's name is his revealed reputation. When his people are defeated, the nations conclude that their God is powerless, and his name is reviled. Ezekiel 36:20-23 gives the same reason for the return: God acts for the sake of his holy name.

nt.note: The Septuagint expanded this line: ‘because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the Gentiles’. Paul quotes that Greek form in Romans 2:24 but turns its meaning. In Isaiah the name is blasphemed because Israel suffers; in Romans it is blasphemed because Jewish teachers of the law break the law they teach. Paul uses Isaiah's words as an indictment rather than a lament, part of his argument that Jew and Gentile alike stand under sin (Romans 3:9).

verses.context: God's answer to the dishonor: on the day he acts, his people will know his name. They will recognize that the one who spoke through the prophets is the one who now stands before them. The verse leads directly into the herald's arrival in verse 7.
verses.grammar: Lakhen, "Therefore", is repeated twice for emphasis. Ani-hu, ‘I am he’, is the formula by which God declares his unique identity in these chapters (41:4, 43:10, 43:13, 46:4, 48:12), rendered in the Septuagint as ego eimi. Hammedabber, "who speaks", is a Piel participle with the article, ‘the one speaking’. The verse ends with hinneni, "here I am", the word servants and prophets use to answer God (Genesis 22:1, 1 Samuel 3:4, Isaiah 6:8), here spoken by God to his people, as again in 58:9 and 65:1.

theology.note: Knowing God's name means knowing him by what he does. The God who spoke beforehand (41:26) proves himself by acting, and his people learn his identity in the event of their rescue. In John's Gospel Jesus uses the same ‘I am he’ formula in ways that echo these chapters (John 8:24, 8:28, 13:19).

verses.context: The scene the whole section has been building toward. A runner appears on the mountains around Jerusalem, and his feet are beautiful because of what he carries: peace, good, salvation, and the message that sums them all up, Your God reigns. Verses 8 to 10 describe the city's response.
verses.grammar: Mah navu, "How beautiful", uses a rare verb form from naah, ‘to be lovely, fitting’. The herald is singular, mevasser, a Piel participle of basar, ‘one bringing good news’ (the BSB's plural "those who bring" generalizes). Three participles describe him: mevasser, ‘announcing’; mashmia, ‘causing to hear’, twice; and omer, ‘saying’. The content grows from shalom, peace, to tov, good, to yeshuah, salvation, to the climactic malakh Elohayikh, "Your God reigns". Malakh is a perfect of the verb ‘to be king’ and can mean ‘has become king’ or ‘reigns’, the cry of the enthronement psalms (Psalm 93:1, 96:10, 97:1).
verses.history: Nahum 1:15 uses almost the same words for the herald who announces the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC. In the Dead Sea Scrolls, 11QMelchizedek (11Q13) quotes this verse and interprets the messenger as ‘the anointed of the Spirit’, linking it with Isaiah 61:1. The Aramaic Targum renders the last line ‘the kingdom of your God has been revealed’, the same phrase it uses elsewhere for God's reign, which shows that by the first centuries AD the verse was being read as announcing the kingdom of God.

theology.note: The good news is that God reigns. Isaiah's herald brings not advice or a program but an announcement of a new state of affairs. Jesus began preaching in Galilee with the same news, that the kingdom of God had come near (Mark 1:14-15), and the New Testament's word for gospel comes from this herald's verb.

nt.note: Paul quotes the verse to show that preachers must be sent: how can they preach unless they are sent, as it is written, how beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news. His wording is closer to the Hebrew than to the Septuagint, whose version of the verse is garbled at this point. Paul makes the herald plural, the messengers of the gospel, and in the next verse quotes Isaiah 53:1 (Romans 10:16), linking the good news of 52:7 directly to the report about the Servant.

verses.context: The watchmen on Jerusalem's walls see the runner and then see what he announces: the LORD himself returning to Zion. They raise their voices together and shout for joy. The return of the exiles is the return of God.
verses.grammar: Qol tsofayikh, "Listen! Your watchmen", is literally ‘the voice of your watchmen’, an exclamation. Tsofeh is the sentry on a city wall who watches for approaching runners (2 Samuel 18:24-27). Ayin beayin yiru, ‘eye to eye they will see’, means they will see directly, face to face, the phrase used in Numbers 14:14 for the LORD being seen eye to eye in the pillar of cloud. Beshuv YHWH Tsiyyon, "when the LORD returns to Zion", uses an infinitive construct of shuv: the LORD returns as the exiles do.
verses.history: The picture of watchmen seeing a runner from far off comes from ordinary military life. In 2 Samuel 18:24-27 David's watchman, on the roof of the gate at Mahanaim, sees two runners approaching and identifies the first by the way he runs before anyone knows the news he carries.

theology.note: Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD leave the temple before its fall (Ezekiel 10:18-19, 11:23) and return to a renewed temple (43:1-5). Isaiah's watchmen see that return. The exile's deepest loss was God's absence; its deepest comfort is his coming back.

verses.context: Even the ruins of Jerusalem are called to sing, because the LORD has comforted and redeemed his people. The comfort commanded in 40:1 has now happened. Verse 10 widens the scene to the whole world: God has rolled up his sleeve before the nations, and the ends of the earth will see his salvation.
verses.grammar: Pitschu rannenu yachdav, "Break forth in joy, sing together", are plural imperatives addressed to the chorvot, the "ruins" of Jerusalem. The reasons are perfects: nicham, ‘he has comforted’ (the verb of 40:1), and gaal, ‘he has redeemed’, the kinsman-redeemer verb of verse 3. In verse 10 chasaf, "has bared", means to strip bare: God pulls his robe back from his arm to act, the gesture of a warrior or a worker (compare Ezekiel 4:7). Zeroa qodsho, "His holy arm", is the exodus arm of 40:10 and will be named again in 53:1. Afsei-arets, "the ends of the earth", is literally ‘the extremities’ of the earth, its farthest edges.

theology.note: Salvation is God's act done in public, before all the nations. The second line of verse 10 is nearly identical to Psalm 98:3. Luke's infancy narrative echoes both halves of these verses: Simeon awaits the consolation of Israel and sees God's salvation prepared before all peoples (Luke 2:25, 2:30-31), and Anna speaks to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (Luke 2:38).

What God does for Jerusalem is meant to be seen by the ends of the earth. The chapter moves from Zion to the nations and then, in verse 15, to the many nations and kings who will be silenced by the Servant.

verses.context: The command to leave Babylon. The exiles are to go out and keep themselves clean, above all those who carry the vessels of the LORD's house back to Jerusalem. The departure is a sacred procession, not an escape.
verses.grammar: Suru suru tseu misham, "Depart, depart, go out from there", doubles its first verb as 51:9 and 52:1 did. Misham, ‘from there’, is pointedly unnamed; the reader knows it is Babylon. Tame al-tiggau, "Touch no unclean thing", is a negated imperfect, a prohibition. Hibbaru, "purify yourselves", is a Niphal imperative of barar, ‘to be clean, pure’. Nosei kelei YHWH, "you who carry the vessels of the LORD", is the description of the Levites' duty in the wilderness (Numbers 4:15).
verses.history: Nebuchadnezzar took the temple's vessels to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13-15), and Belshazzar's feast used them (Daniel 5:2-3). Ezra 1:7-11 records that Cyrus returned them to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah, and lists them by kind, a total of 5,400 articles of gold and silver brought up from Babylon to Jerusalem with the exiles.

theology.note: Leaving Babylon is not only a change of address but a separation from its uncleanness. The New Testament applies the call to the church's separation from idolatry (2 Corinthians 6:17) and to God's people coming out of the Babylon of Revelation (Revelation 18:4).

nt.note: Paul strings together several Old Testament texts (Leviticus 26:12, this verse, Ezekiel 20:34, and 2 Samuel 7:14) to call the Corinthians away from partnership with idolatry: come out from their midst and be separate, touch no unclean thing, and I will welcome you. He applies Isaiah's call to leave Babylon to Christians who must separate not from a place but from the worship of idols, because they are God's temple (6:16).

verses.context: The new exodus will not be like the first. Israel left Egypt in haste; they will leave Babylon unhurried, with the LORD going ahead of them and guarding them from behind. The verse closes the scene of the herald, and the next verse abruptly introduces the Servant.
verses.grammar: Lo vechippazon tetseu, "you will not leave in a hurry": chippazon, ‘haste’, occurs only here and in the Passover texts, where Israel eats the Passover in haste (Exodus 12:11) and leaves Egypt in haste (Deuteronomy 16:3). The echo is deliberate: this exodus reverses the first in its manner. Holekh lifneikhem YHWH, ‘going before you is the LORD’, and umeassifkhem Elohei Yisrael, "the God of Israel is your rear guard", use participles; measef, ‘one who gathers’, is the rear guard that collects stragglers, the position held by Dan's tribe on the march (Numbers 10:25).

theology.note: God surrounds his people on the road, before and behind, as the pillar of cloud moved from the front of Israel's column to the rear at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:19). Isaiah 58:8 uses the same picture: the glory of the LORD will be your rear guard.

verses.context: The fourth Servant Song begins, and God himself speaks: behold my Servant. The first line announces the end before the story: the Servant will succeed and be exalted to the highest place. Only then does the song turn, in verse 14, to the disfigurement that preceded the exaltation. The song runs to 53:12.
verses.grammar: Hinneh, "Behold", calls attention as in 42:1, where the first Servant Song began the same way. Yaskil, "will prosper", is a Hiphil of sakhal, which means both to act wisely and to succeed as a result (Joshua 1:8; Jeremiah 23:5 uses it of the righteous Branch who will reign wisely). Three verbs of height follow: yarum, ‘he will be high’; venissa, ‘and lifted up’; vegavah meod, ‘and exalted greatly’. The first two, rum and nasa, are paired elsewhere in Isaiah for God enthroned: Isaiah saw the Lord ram venissa, ‘high and lifted up’ (6:1), and 57:15 names God ‘the high and lofty One’ with the same two words (compare 33:10). In 2:12-14 the pair describes the proud human heights God brings low. The Servant is exalted in the vocabulary of God's own majesty, and without the pride that vocabulary condemns in humans.
verses.text: The Septuagint renders the verbs ‘my servant will understand, and will be lifted up (hypsothesetai) and glorified (doxasthesetai) exceedingly’. The Aramaic Targum identifies him explicitly: ‘Behold, my servant the Messiah will prosper’. The Targum then reassigns the song's sufferings to Israel and the nations while giving the exaltation to the Messiah.

theology.note: The Servant's story is told from its ending: whatever follows in the song, God's verdict is that he will be exalted. The New Testament reads the resurrection and ascension of Jesus as exactly that verdict (Philippians 2:9).

The Servant is not called king or Messiah in the song itself, and interpreters debate whether he is Israel, the prophet, or a future individual (see the notes on chapter 53). But the Targum's messianic reading, and the song's use of the language of God's own exaltation, show why Jewish and Christian readers alike heard a figure greater than any prophet.

nt.note: John's Gospel repeatedly speaks of the Son of Man being ‘lifted up’ (3:14, 8:28, 12:32-34) and ‘glorified’ (12:23, 13:31), the two Greek verbs of the Septuagint of this verse, and uses them for the cross itself. In 12:38-41 John quotes Isaiah 53:1 and 6:10 together and says Isaiah saw his glory. Richard Bauckham has argued that John read Isaiah 52:13 and 6:1 together, since both use ‘high and lifted up’, and so found in Isaiah a vision of the crucified Servant sharing God's throne.

Peter tells the crowd in the temple that the God of Abraham has glorified his servant (pais) Jesus, using the Septuagint's word for glorified and the title Servant from this verse, and then speaks of the one they delivered over and denied.

verses.context: The song's first reversal. Many were appalled at the Servant, because his appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man. The verse is the ‘just as’ half of a comparison whose ‘so’ comes in verse 15: just as many were horrified at him, so he will astonish many nations.
verses.grammar: Kaasher shamemu alekha rabbim, ‘just as many were appalled at you’: shamem is to be devastated or aghast, used of the horror onlookers feel at a ruin (1 Kings 9:8, Jeremiah 18:16). The Hebrew has ‘at you’, a sudden second person that interrupts God's description; some ancient witnesses, the Syriac among them, read ‘at him’, and the BSB follows them. The dash in the BSB marks a parenthesis: ken-mishchat meish marehu, ‘so marred beyond a man was his appearance, and his form beyond the sons of Adam’. Mishchat, ‘disfigurement’, is a noun from shachat, ‘to ruin, corrupt’, the word for spoiled or blemished offerings in Leviticus 22:25. Ken, ‘so’, is used twice in this sentence, once inside the parenthesis and once at the start of verse 15.
verses.text: The great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (1QIsaa) reads mashachti, ‘I anointed’, where the Masoretic Text has mishchat, ‘disfigurement’. The two words look alike and share consonants except for a final letter. On the scroll's reading the line becomes ‘so I anointed his appearance beyond any man’. William H. Brownlee argued that this reading was original and messianic; most scholars regard it as a variant spelling or a scribal change and keep the Masoretic reading, which fits ‘appalled’ and the song's theme of a disfigured Servant.

theology.note: The Servant's suffering is not hidden or softened; it makes onlookers recoil. The Gospels describe the flogging, the crown of thorns, and the beating of Jesus with restraint (Mark 15:15-20), but the song prepares readers for the shock of a Messiah whose appearance repels.

verses.context: The second half of the comparison. As many were appalled at the Servant, so he will affect many nations, and kings will shut their mouths before him. The reason: they will see what they were never told and understand what they never heard. The stanza ends in astonished silence, and 53:1 asks who has believed the report.
verses.grammar: The key verb is yazzeh, a Hiphil imperfect of nazah. Everywhere else nazah means to sprinkle or spatter a liquid, blood, water, or oil, in the rites of purification and atonement (Leviticus 4:6, 14:7, 16:14; Numbers 19:18-19). In those texts the liquid is the object and the person or thing is sprinkled ‘on’ (with the preposition al); here goyim rabbim, "many nations", is the direct object with no preposition, which is unusual on the sprinkling reading. Two main translations result. Sprinkle (the KJV, NASB, ESV, and BSB) takes the Servant as a priest who cleanses the nations, a sense that anticipates 53:10's guilt offering. Startle (the RSV, NRSV, and the Jewish Publication Society's 1985 translation) takes yazzeh from a different root, known from Arabic, meaning to leap, so ‘cause to leap up’ in astonishment; this matches the parallel with "appalled" in verse 14 and the silenced kings in the next line, and follows the Septuagint's ‘many nations will marvel at him’. Yiqpetsu malakhim pihem, ‘kings will shut their mouths’, is a gesture of awed silence (Job 29:9-10). The last lines contrast perfects: what was not recounted (suppar) to them they see (rau), what they had not heard they understand (hitbonanu).

theology.note: On the reading ‘sprinkle’, the Servant does for the nations what the priest did for Israel: he makes them clean. Hebrews speaks of hearts sprinkled clean (10:22) and of the sprinkled blood of Jesus (12:24), and 1 Peter 1:2 of sprinkling with his blood. On the reading ‘startle’, the atoning work is stated in chapter 53 rather than here. Either way, the song's opening already reaches beyond Israel to many nations.
The Servant's work reaches kings and nations who were never told of him. Paul made the second half of this verse his missionary principle: to preach where Christ had not been named (Romans 15:20-21).

nt.note: Paul quotes the second half of the verse from the Septuagint, which adds ‘about him’: those who were not told about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand. He uses it to explain why he has aimed to preach the gospel where Christ has not already been named, so as not to build on another's foundation (15:20). Paul reads the nations' astonished understanding as the result of his own apostolic preaching of the Servant, Jesus.
